And you know, structural collapse is such a terrifying thing. When a building fails, it's almost never just one thing. It's a cascade of failures. First a beam gives way because of metal fatigue, and then the load transfers to the adjacent columns, and if they aren't rated for that kind of stress, they buckle. It's called progressive collapse. That's what happened with the Twin Towers, actually. The heat from the fire weakened the steel trusses, and once one floor pancaked onto the next, the kinetic energy was just too massive for the lower floors to withstand. I actually did my senior thesis on progressive collapse and load redistribution in high-rise structures. I built this scale model out of balsa wood and tested it with different weight distributions. But yeah, the money would help, obviously. But I don't think it would fix this... this feeling of just being buried under the wreckage.

Dread is an interesting concept, psychologically speaking, but in engineering, we deal with a different kind of dread. The dread of catastrophic failure. It's why we have safety factors built into every calculation. You never design a structure to just barely hold the expected load; you design it to hold two, three, sometimes five times that amount, depending on the application. Like elevators. The cables on an elevator are usually designed with a safety factor of eleven. Eleven! That means a single cable could hold eleven times the weight of a fully loaded car, and most elevators have four to eight cables. It's incredibly redundant. But people still get terrified of getting in them. They watch too many movies where the cables snap and the car goes into freefall. But the truth is, even if all the cables snapped—which is statistically nearly impossible—Elisha Otis invented the safety hoist back in 1852. It's a mechanical braking system that engages automatically if the car falls too fast. It wedges into the guide rails in the shaft. It's a brilliant piece of engineering, really. So simple, but it completely changed the modern city. We wouldn't have skyscrapers without it. 

But anyway, no, I wouldn't say I'm feeling on edge like I'm about to jump out of my skin. Just... weighed down by everything.

But now they cover everything from financial counseling to mental health crises. It's a smart investment for companies, really, when you look at the cost-benefit analysis. The cost of replacing a specialized employee—especially in engineering, where you have to factor in recruitment, onboarding, and the loss of institutional knowledge—is astronomical. It can be up to 200% of their annual salary. So paying a third-party vendor a few dollars per employee per month for an EAP is just basic risk mitigation. It's like installing a pressure relief valve on a boiler. You hope you never need it, but if the pressure builds up too high, you absolutely want it there to prevent a catastrophic explosion. Boilers are terrifying if they aren't maintained properly. Water expands 1,600 times its volume when it turns to steam. If a boiler ruptures, it can level an entire building. There was a famous explosion at a shoe factory in Brockton, Massachusetts, in 1905... a boiler blew up and the building collapsed, and then caught fire. turns.doctor_question: During this past month, have you been worrying a lot?
turns.patient_response:
I don't think I've been worrying, exactly. Like I said, it's more of that heavy, dreadful feeling, rather than my mind racing with specific worries about things. I just... I don't care enough to worry, if that makes sense. It's just blank.

Blankness is actually a huge problem in material science, though we usually call it voids. When you're pouring concrete, for example, if it's not vibrated properly, you get these air pockets or voids trapped inside the forms. We call it honeycombing. It looks exactly like it sounds, just this porous, brittle mess on the surface of the concrete. It completely compromises the structural integrity because those voids create stress concentrations. The compressive strength just plummets. And repairing it is a nightmare. You have to chip away all the defective concrete until you hit sound material, and then patch it with a high-strength grout, but the bond between the old concrete and the new patch is always a weak point. It's never as strong as a monolithic pour. That's why inspectors are so obsessive about slump tests and watching the vibration process during a pour. A single bad truckload of concrete can ruin a bridge pier. I actually had a project a few years ago where we had to reject three trucks in a row because the slump was completely off—they added way too much water at the batch plant. Water-cement ratio is everything. 

But no, my mind hasn't been racing with worries. Just... empty.
